Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Italy. Legal with prescription (ricetta medica). Italy requires original packaging and a medical certificate for travelers carrying controlled medications.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Italy. Amphetamines are in Table I of Italy's controlled substances (DPR 309/1990). Adderall is not approved or marketed in Italy. Importing is illegal and can result in criminal prosecution.

Cannabis / CBD is restricted in Italy. Medical cannabis available since 2013 with specialist prescription. Recreational use decriminalized for small amounts (administrative sanctions). CBD products with <0.6% THC legally sold as 'cannabis light.'

Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) is restricted in Italy. Available by prescription for ADHD but heavily regulated (Table I substance requiring special prescription). Must carry original packaging and medical documentation.

Codeine / opioids is restricted in Italy. Low-dose codeine available with standard prescription. Stronger opioids require special non-repeatable prescriptions (ricetta non ripetibile). Subject to strict dispensing controls.
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is caution in Italy. Available OTC from pharmacies in limited quantities. No special restrictions beyond standard pharmacy sale, but large quantities may raise questions.

Psilocybin / MDMA is banned in Italy. Both classified as Table I narcotics. Possession of any amount is illegal; personal use quantities receive administrative sanctions, larger amounts carry criminal penalties.
Tramadol is restricted in Italy. Prescription required. Available with standard medical prescription. Carry original packaging and documentation when traveling.
Tranquilizers / sleeping pills (zolpidem) is restricted in Italy. Available by prescription. Zolpidem requires a non-repeatable prescription (ricetta non ripetibile). Must carry documentation.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The SS163 Private-Transfer & Abusivo-Taxi Gouge (transport, severity: high). Unlicensed and licensed drivers on the SS163 Amalfi Drive — the 50km coastal road linking Sorrento, Positano, Praiano, Amalfi and Ravello — quote flat rates that run 20–30x the SITA bus fare. Traveler reports document firsthand trips: Sorrento → Praiano (23km) quoted at €120, Praiano → Ravello (14km) at €120 'cheap compared to the €180 our hotel offered.' A separate 2025 trip report from Minori records Positano → Amalfi quoted at €200 and Amalfi → Minori (5km) at €50. Fanpage's 'Tassisti abusivi dal Napoletano ad Amalfi per truffare i turisti' documents a carabinieri operation that sanctioned 6 abusivi working Amalfi, Ravello and the coast — drivers with no taxi license operating from Naples province into the costiera specifically to intercept cruise-ship passengers at Molo Pennello. Positanonews' 'Salerno. Taxi abusivi, affare lucroso senza rischi e tasse' quotes Orsa Taxi: the abusivo 'proposes a transfer that looks cheaper than a licensed taxi,' then overcharges and leaves no receipt. How to avoid: Take the SITA Sud bus — €2.10 at any tabaccheria — for Sorrento → Positano → Amalfi; or the Alilauro/Travelmar ferry (€20–25 one-way) for an equally scenic, reliable option that bypasses the road entirely. If you need a private driver for Path of the Gods access or a full day, book a licensed NCC through your hotel with a written quote in Euros, full itinerary, all stops and return time fixed before you leave — budget €350–500 for a full-day Positano/Amalfi/Ravello loop. Refuse any driver at Amalfi Molo Pennello, Sorrento station forecourt or a hotel lobby who offers 'special price' verbally with no written contract. Confirm the vehicle has a visible TAXI or NCC roof sign and civic license number before boarding. Demand a ricevuta with driver's name, license plate, route and total — without it, no complaint to the vigili urbani will stick.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The Marina Grande Boat-Charter & 'Private Tour' Overcharge (overcharging, severity: high). Day-charter operators on Marina Grande in Amalfi, Marina di Praia in Praiano and the small quays in Positano quote €500–1,500/day to small groups for what the same licensed gozzo boat sells for €300–600 directly. The scam layers on top: 'guides' at Amalfi Molo Pennello with clipboards intercept cruise passengers and resell Viator/GetYourGuide vouchers at 2–3x their online price; fuel, lunch stops and Capri Blue Grotto entry are quoted as 'included' then charged separately at the end; and unlicensed captains without a ministerial commercial license operate alongside licensed ones, leaving passengers with no insurance if anything goes wrong. A 2025 Amalfi Coast excursion thread records a Cobalto Boat Escapes full-day private charter at a 'fair' rate — the going benchmark for legitimate operators. Traveler reports name Restart Boats for Capri boat days as reputable; anonymous clipboard sellers at the marina pitching 'the same tour, €100 cheaper' are the ones to avoid. How to avoid: Book the boat charter online before you arrive — reputable operators (Cobalto, Restart, Lucibello, Mare di Praia) publish rates, include fuel and skipper, and deliver a PDF contract with the itinerary. Never hand cash to a man with a clipboard at Marina Grande or Molo Pennello; always pay the operator directly at their branded kiosk. Confirm what's included in writing: fuel, captain, lunch, drinks, Blue Grotto entry (€18 extra per person), snorkelling gear. Verify the captain's commercial license — a legitimate commercial skipper displays his 'patente nautica commerciale' on request. If a cruise-ship day is tight, use the ship's shore-excursion desk rather than a clipboard hawker at the pier; shore excursions are vetted and the ship won't leave without you.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The Sea-View Coperto & Pesce "al Etto" Trap (overcharging, severity: high). Restaurants along the Amalfi lungomare, Atrani's tiny piazza, Positano's Spiaggia Grande, and the Ravello belvederes layer four overcharges on sunset-chasing tourists: an unmarked per-person coperto of €4–6 (versus the €2–3 norm inland), a 15% 'servizio' added automatically to foreign cards, pane/acqua/antipasti arriving without being ordered, and — the biggest hit — fish and seafood priced 'al etto' (per 100g) on the menu that arrives as a 400–700g whole fish billed at 4–7x what the diner expected. A 2025 firsthand traveler post documents a frozen-food tourist-trap restaurant where 'the price on the menu is one, at the register it's another' and waiters surround diners at the bill to prevent them leaving. Community advice from Italian locals warns explicitly about 'fish priced per etto' as the flagship Italian-coast restaurant trap. Positanonews' 2019 'Vietri sul Mare, truffa ex Pergola' records a decade-long court case against a coastal restaurant's operators for systematic tourist fraud. Italian law requires prices posted outside the door — an Amalfi sea-view terrace with no posted menu is legally non-compliant. How to avoid: Photograph the posted menu from outside before you sit — if fish or steak has no per-item price and is only listed 'al etto,' ask the waiter to weigh and quote the specific fish before cooking, in writing if needed. Ask at seating: 'mi conferma il coperto, il servizio, e il prezzo del pesce che ho ordinato?' Refuse any pane, acqua, or antipasti you didn't order — Italian law lets you send them back without charge. Walk one street uphill: in Amalfi, the trattorias on Via Capuano and Via delle Cartiere are locally priced; in Atrani, Piazza Umberto I sits above the tourist circuit; in Ravello, skip the Piazza Duomo perimeter for venues a block off. Check Italian-language Google reviews sorted by 'Più recenti' — a venue rated 4.5+ by Italians and 3.8 by English speakers is authentic; the reverse is a trap.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The Amalfi & Ravello Parcheggiatori Abusivi (transport, severity: high). Unofficial 'attendants' in fluorescent vests at Amalfi's Piazza Flavio Gioia seafront, Atrani's Spiaggia, the Ravello approach via Viale Richard Wagner, and the Positano Chiesa Nuova hill wave rental cars into 'reserved' spots they do not own, then demand €15–30 in cash — well above the legitimate municipal rate (Piazza Flavio Gioia pay-and-display runs roughly €5/hour). Fanpage's 2024 Guardia di Finanza and carabinieri blitz reporting on the Penisola Sorrentina and costiera documents parcheggiatori abusivi as one of the two priority enforcement targets (the other being abusivi taxi drivers). Traveler reports from Cefalù document the ZTL sister pattern: rental cars drifting into resident-only zones and attracting €55+ camera-issued fines laundered through the rental company after the trip. In Amalfi specifically, cars parked in spaces 'assigned' by the unofficial attendant are frequently ticketed anyway because the attendant had no authority — the tourist pays twice. How to avoid: Park only at the official Luna Rossa and Piazza Flavio Gioia municipal lots in Amalfi (pay-and-display machine with Italian-language instructions), the signed Positano lots on the main highway (drop down by foot), the Ravello car parks at Piazza del Duomo and Auditorium Niemeyer, or your hotel's own garage with a written space included in the room rate. Refuse any man in a vest who approaches your moving car — they have no legal authority and do not issue valid receipts. If cornered, pay only €1–2 'mancia' (tip) rather than the €15–30 demanded — most will accept rather than escalate. Photograph any vest-wearing 'attendant' and the surrounding signs before paying; file a report at the Comune di Amalfi's vigili urbani office if threatened. Consider skipping the rental car entirely — the SITA bus and ferry cover every town on the coast.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The "Antica" Limoncello Shop & Factory-Tour Upsell (overcharging, severity: medium). Shops along Amalfi's Via Lorenzo d'Amalfi and Piazza Duomo, Positano's Via dei Mulini, and Sorrento's Via San Cesareo (a common day-trip endpoint) sell 'family recipe since 1800s' limoncello at €18–35 for 500ml — the same IGP Costa d'Amalfi limoncello sells for €6–10 at any inland alimentari or supermarket. The upsell is a free tasting that softens the buyer before the register. A common variant: a 'private factory tour' pitched by a taxi or tour driver at €30–60/person that delivers a 15-minute walkthrough of a showroom attached to a souvenir shop, the driver taking a commission on the purchase. Traveler reports name La Valle dei Mulini (amalfilemon.it), and the shop past the Amalfi basilica and paper factory, as reputable — these publish their prices online. Positanonews' long-running coverage of costiera food fraud contextualises the broader pattern: real Limoncello di Amalfi IGP must carry the consortium's numbered seal; many shop bottles sold as 'Amalfi' limoncello are produced in Salerno province with unregulated lemons. How to avoid: Check any bottle for the IGP 'Limoncello Costa d'Amalfi' consortium seal before paying €20+ — without it, you are buying unregulated generic limoncello at a tourist markup. Compare prices at a random inland alimentari or a Coop / Conad supermarket in Amalfi town first (€6–10 for 500ml of a perfectly good brand). For factory visits, walk to La Valle dei Mulini (free, up the path past Amalfi basilica) rather than paying €30+ for a driver-escorted 'private tour.' Refuse 'commission tours' sold by taxi or NCC drivers — legitimate tours are bookable direct with the producer at publishing rates. If you want a single nice bottle as a gift, pick one with the IGP seal from a named producer (Valle dei Mulini, Villa Massa, Pallini) — avoid generic 'Antica' branding with no consortium mark.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The SITA Bus Ticket & Board-Without-Ticket Confusion (transport, severity: medium). SITA Sud — the €2.10 bus line connecting Sorrento, Positano, Praiano, Amalfi, Atrani, Minori, Maiori and Vietri — requires tickets purchased from a tabaccheria before boarding, validated in the on-bus machine. Tourists who board without a pre-bought ticket are told by the driver in rapid Italian that 'tickets are not sold on board,' then a controllore appears 10 minutes later and issues a €55–200 fine. Traveler reports from 2024 document a related pattern — Florence-based but the same across Italy — where tourists were blocked from exiting and coerced into paying a fine at a handheld terminal. A 2024 Amalfi-transit post records SITA buses 'not stopping when full' and 'passing tourists by' during peak hours, pushing travelers to pay scalpers for 'day passes' that turn out to be the same €2.10 fare sold at €10. The legitimate SITA day pass ('Unico Costiera' 24-hour) costs €10 and is only sold at tabaccherie and SITA kiosks — not by street sellers. How to avoid: Buy SITA tickets at any tabaccheria before boarding — the €2.10 single or the €10 Unico Costiera 24-hour day pass. Validate the ticket in the orange on-bus machine the moment you step on; keep the validated stub until you exit. Ignore anyone selling 'day passes' or 'bus tickets' at the stop who is not inside a tabaccheria — they are either resellers marking up the fare or handing you invalid tickets. If the bus is full and driver refuses boarding, walk 200m further along the route: on the SS163, a second or third bus usually follows within 20–40 minutes, and many stops sit between bends where you can flag one outside the main queue. For reliability at peak times, Mobility Amalfi Coast (mobilityamalficoast.com) offers reservable seats on smaller buses at a modest markup — a legitimate alternative to waiting hours in a SITA line.

Scam alert in Amalfi Coast, Italy — The Fake Villa Rental & Off-Platform Wire (money, severity: high). Fraudulent 'villa' and 'apartment' listings for the Amalfi Coast — Airbnb, Booking, Vrbo, and standalone websites with generic names — direct guests off-platform via email or WhatsApp for a 'discount' or 'to avoid platform fees,' take a bank transfer or cryptocurrency, then vanish on arrival day. A 2024 traveler thread on livingAmalfi.com captures the anxious pattern: travelers second-guessing standalone booking sites whose names sound plausible but offer no platform protection. The Amalfi Coast's extreme supply/demand imbalance — peak-season studios at €500/night and up — is the soil the scam grows in: a 'villa with pool for €180/night' lure is cheaper than any real listing should be, and the urgency push ('three other parties asking about the dates') is the tell. The pattern repeats the Bologna Fiera-district scam documented on TripAdvisor's 'Be aware of scams' forum thread: off-platform email contact ('Bjarne'), pressure to wire a deposit, 'SCAM. DO NOT BOOK' review on arrival. Campania's 2025 Meta tourism-tax increase (up to €4/night, published by Metropolis) is now used as a fake 'city fee in cash' cover at arrival. How to avoid: Book only on Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo or another platform with pay-through-the-platform guarantees — never wire money or pay cryptocurrency to a private bank account for an Amalfi Coast rental, no matter how compelling the 'discount' pitch. Reverse-image-search every interior photo; scam listings reuse photos from legitimate properties in Positano, Sorrento, or as far away as Greece. Check the property on Google Street View — a legitimate Amalfi Coast villa has a visible gate and address. Require the host to message you inside the platform's chat system with a photo of the entrance and key-handoff procedure; scammers refuse because it breaks their anonymity. Budget for the legitimate imposta di soggiorno (€2–4/night in 2025–26, varies by comune) — any host adding a surprise 'city fee in cash' above that is pocketing it. Push back on 'credit card surcharges' — EU PSD2 bars them on most consumer cards.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Via dell'Indipendenza "Cigarette" Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). Pairs of women on Via dell'Indipendenza interrupt tourists asking for a cigarette, the time, or directions while a partner pickpockets the wallet or bag. A June 2016 Il Resto del Carlino arrest documented two Roma women (ages 18 and 26) using this exact MO on a Japanese tourist; a September 2025 firsthand traveler post and an August 2025 CCTV arrest on Via Riva di Reno confirm the female-duo pattern is still active in 2025. How to avoid: On Via dell'Indipendenza, walk on the portico-wall side with your bag between you and the wall. Reply to any 'posso fare una domanda' with a firm 'no, mi scusi' and keep walking. Use a crossbody bag with the zipper facing your body. Shout 'ladri!' if a theft is in progress — Bologna police actively patrol this street. Never carry a wallet in a back pocket in the historic center.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Due Torri "Spare Some Change" Arm-Grab (pickpocket, severity: high). Beggars at Piazza di Porta Ravegnana — directly under the Torre degli Asinelli and Torre Garisenda — grab tourists' arms during a pretended plea for alms and empty pockets in the same motion. An August 2016 Il Resto del Carlino arrest (44-year-old Bosnian woman with prior convictions, 6pm, Spanish tourist) established the MO; a Bolognatoday report of a Japanese tourist restraining a thief in the same piazza confirms it repeats. A 3am variant turns violent — a 43-year-old French woman was slapped and robbed in the historic center. How to avoid: Compose your upward-looking tower photo before stopping — phone out, zip closed, bag in hand. Step back one full pace if anyone making a begging gesture enters your body space. Never let a stranger touch you in the historic center. Carry a daily-use wallet with €40–€60 and keep cards, passport, and larger cash in a flat pouch under your shirt. Call 112 immediately if robbed.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — Bologna Centrale Platform & Taxi-Queue Pickpockets (pickpocket, severity: high). Coordinated groups work Bologna Centrale platforms, underground passages, ticket machines and the taxi queue. Train staff now announce 'attenzione, pickpocket!' as trains pull in. A July 2024 incident saw a Business-class suitcase stolen from a Frecciarossa during the ~10-minute Bologna Centrale stop. Variants include 'helper' scams at FastTicket kiosks that photograph card PINs and three-to-five-person distraction teams that open outer luggage pouches on platforms. How to avoid: Exit via the main Piazza delle Medaglie d'Oro entrance, not Via Carracci (Bolognina/rear). Take only official white taxis from the signed rank; ignore any 'taxi?' offers inside the hall. Use only Trenitalia or Italo apps or their logo-marked machines for tickets. Keep luggage on the facing end-of-carriage rack on Frecciarossa/Italo. Never buy tickets from third-party resellers.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Outdoor Restaurant Bag-Snatch (theft, severity: high). Bags hung on chair backs at outdoor Quadrilatero and Jewish Ghetto restaurants are snatched by passing pedestrians, followed by immediate ATM cashout before cards can be frozen. A June 2017 Il Resto del Carlino arrest documented a 22-year-old Moroccan man snatching a 53-year-old American tourist's purse on Via Volturno; police caught him on Via dei Mille with her Gucci wallet, €70 cash, credit cards, and a $500 check. A Bolognatoday 'Furto nel Ghetto' report documents the ATM-cashout variant on Via de' Giudei. How to avoid: Place your bag on the floor with one strap looped around your chair leg or ankle — never on the chair back or an empty seat. Sit with your back to a wall facing foot traffic. Leave your passport in the hotel safe. Use in-app card blocks immediately if a bag disappears — the ATM variant depends on a 3–10 minute reaction lag. Eat where locals eat; avoid the Piazza-Maggiore-to-Piazza-della-Mercanzia alleys flagged by locals as '95% tourist traps'.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Bologna Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Bologna Airport drivers quote flat fares above the posted €12.80 fixed fare (up to 6km) or switch the meter to a long-distance tariff inside the city. A 2025 traveler thread documents a €24 starting fare — a fellow commenter calls it 'straight up scammed.' The true max radio starting fare is €6.80; per-km is €1.45 in normal daytime. Variants include the 'credit card reader is broken' scam that forces victims to withdraw cash at ATMs while the driver watches the PIN. How to avoid: Use the Marconi Express monorail (€12.20, ~7 minutes) from the airport to Bologna Centrale — it is faster and has nothing to negotiate. For taxis, use only white-painted Cotabo or Taxi Bologna at the official rank and confirm the €12.80 airport fixed fare before closing the door. Use TaxiClick or Cotabo (051.372727) for radio calls. Always demand a ricevuta with taxi number, time, and route. Refuse any ATM detour.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Quadrilatero "Ancient" Tourist-Menu Trap (overcharging, severity: moderate). Quadrilatero restaurants add unmarked per-person coperto (often above €3.50), automatic 15% 'servizio' on foreign cards, unrequested pane/acqua/antipasti, and fish or steak priced 'al etto' that arrives at 400–600g. A 2024 NYT opinion piece documents 'Ancient cold cuts butcher' chain shops that had actually 'been open for three months.' Locals name the Piazza-Maggiore-to-Piazza-della-Mercanzia alleys as '95% tourist traps.' How to avoid: Walk 3–5 minutes off the Piazza Maggiore axis — Via del Pratello, Santo Stefano, or Mercato delle Erbe are locally recommended. Photograph the posted menu outside before sitting (Italian law requires prices). Ask at seating: 'mi conferma il coperto e se c'è servizio?' Prefer trattorias/osterias with handwritten daily menus. Trust Italian-language Google reviews sorted by Most Recent over English reviews.

Scam alert in Bologna, Italy — The Fake Short-Term-Rental / Key Handoff (money, severity: high). Fraudulent hosts on Airbnb, Booking and TripAdvisor direct guests off-platform for payment, then vanish on arrival day. TripAdvisor Bologna Forum's 'Be aware of scams' thread documents a victim contacted by 'Bjarne' via off-platform email; a 'SCAM. DO NOT BOOK' review names a Fiera-district apartment that was locked and unresponsive on arrival. Side patterns: undisclosed credit-card surcharges and a fake 'city tax in cash' cover (Bologna's real €5/night tourism tax applies only to rooms over €120/night). How to avoid: Book only through Airbnb, Booking.com, or platforms with pay-through-platform guarantees — never wire or pay cash off-platform. Check the property on Google Street View before arrival. Require in-platform messages with photos of the entrance and keybox. Budget for the €5/night tourism tax (rooms over €120/night only); refuse cash 'city fee' surprises. Push back on credit-card surcharges — EU PSD2 bars them on most consumer cards and legitimate B&Bs don't ask.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — The Blue Grotto (Grotta Azzurra) Fee Stack (overcharging, severity: high). Capri's signature scam is not a single overcharge — it is a stack of four separate fees that tourists assume are bundled: roughly €18 for the small transfer boat out to the grotto mouth, €18 for the mandatory rowboat and Cooperativa Battellieri Capresi entry, a customary €2–€5 tip the rower will state out loud, and a €2 Comune tax. Families routinely leave having paid €35–€45 per person for what they thought was a €15 ticket. Worse, if the sea is too rough or the grotto is closed, many island 'giro + Blue Grotto' operators still charge the boat-tour fare and issue no refund — Capri.it and TripAdvisor reviews call it 'Truffa al 100%' and a 'La Truffa Azzurra' scam after the cave's name. An August 2024 viral Ferragosto video showed two rival boatmen in a fist-fight at the grotto mouth in front of tourists, reported by regional politician Francesco Emilio Borrelli and covered by Fanpage. How to avoid: Take the ATC #3 bus from Anacapri to the Grotta Azzurra stop and descend to the sea-level landing; from there you only pay the rowboat + entry fee, skipping the transfer boat. Confirm in advance — call the Cooperativa Battellieri or check capri.com — whether the grotto is open that day before paying any boat-tour fare; sea conditions close it often. Decline the tip if service is aggressive; it is legally optional. Never buy 'Blue Grotto included' boat-tour packages without explicit refund terms in writing. If the operator refuses a refund when the grotto is closed, keep the receipt and file a complaint with the Comune di Capri or Guardia Costiera.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — Marina Grande Hydrofoil & Ferry Ticket Markup (transport, severity: moderate). Unofficial 'guides' and tour touts at Marina Grande sell marked-up Capri↔Naples and Capri↔Sorrento hydrofoil tickets that should be bought directly at the Caremar, Alilauro, SNAV, NLG or Gescab counters or on FerryHopper/operator apps. A separate Amalfi Coast travel group Facebook post in 2025 titled 'Beware of ticket scams in Capri' documents ticket-inspector-plus-driver collusion on island buses, with tourists fined for 'invalid' tickets the driver had just sold them. Traveler reports on NLG confirm that e-tickets from the operators' apps are sufficient and no third-party collection is needed — paid vouchers are pure markup. How to avoid: Buy Caremar, Alilauro, SNAV, NLG or Gescab tickets only at the signed window offices on Marina Grande's pier or through FerryHopper / the operator's own app. Decline any 'combined ticket' a stranger pushes on the jetty — these carry €5–€20 markups. On island ATC buses, buy the paper ticket from the official tobacconist (tabacchi) in Marina Grande, Capri Town, or Anacapri before boarding, and validate it immediately in the on-bus machine; never buy tickets from the driver if an alternative exists, and keep the validated ticket on you for the full ride. Strikes and weather-closure disruptions happen frequently — use FerryHopper's strike alerts before your outbound ferry.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — Unlicensed Boat-Charter & Island-Tour Gouge (overcharging, severity: high). Private 'Capri giro dell'isola' boat charters quoted in the €400–€1,500/day range with hidden fuel surcharges (€35/person), undisclosed €15/person 'tourist tax to Capri,' and no refund when the boat is cancelled for 'wind' while identical boats visibly leave the marina. TripAdvisor reviews of Capri private-charter operators document €389 gozzo charters cancelled for alleged wind while other boats departed normally, with reviewers concluding the operator had found 'qualche turista dalle uova d'oro pronto a pagarli di più' (a golden-goose tourist willing to pay more). Traveler reports warn of the identical pattern for private boat tours departing from Positano and Amalfi to Capri. How to avoid: Only book boat charters through operators with a visible Capitaneria di Porto license number and a written itinerary that lists: total price, fuel surcharge, tourist tax, mooring fees, tender fees (especially to Da Luigi ai Faraglioni, €10/person each way), cancellation terms, and refund terms if the sea is declared 'mosso.' Pay by credit card, never cash, so you can chargeback. Take a public scheduled 'giro dell'isola' (Motoscafisti di Capri and similar licensed co-ops) for €20–€25/person rather than a private charter if you don't need privacy. Compare any private quote to those posted rates — a private gozzo over €500/day for 6 hours is priced for tourists. Never pay in cash to a beach promoter.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — The Piazzetta Café Bill Shock (overcharging, severity: moderate). La Piazzetta — Piazza Umberto I — is Capri's famous 'salotto del mondo' and its most visible tourist-café strip. In July 2022, RaiNews published a receipt showing a €78 breakfast at a Piazzetta bar for six cornetti, three espressi, one cappuccino and two latte macchiato — roughly €13 per person, with one cornetto priced at €5.50. A viral Tele Italia video titled 'Capri, la colazione in Piazzetta costa 78 euro' drove the story internationally. The charges are technically legal because a tariff is posted (usually the 'al bar' standing-price menu on an interior wall), but the outdoor 'al tavolo' tariff is often not visible from the table and not quoted by the waiter; tourists who order at the bar and then carry drinks to a table are still upcharged. The trap is the absence of per-item table prices at the outdoor seating itself. How to avoid: Before sitting at any Piazzetta outdoor table, ask 'che prezzo ha al tavolo?' (what's the table price?) and have the waiter point to the posted price list. The bar (standing) price is often a third of the table price — order and drink at the bar to pay the posted €2–€4 espresso instead of €8–€15. If you want the Piazzetta view-sit, budget €15–€25 per drink as the real cost and confirm per-item table prices before ordering. Walk 200m off the Piazzetta toward Via Le Botteghe or Via Camerelle for cafes with published table menus. Never order 'anything the waiter recommends' without a price quote — that is when shock bills of €35 cocktails appear.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — The Faraglioni Beach Club Minimum-Spend Trap (overcharging, severity: high). Capri has effectively no free public beach with comfortable access — so the Faraglioni-facing private beach clubs effectively monopolise the 'lie-down-by-the-sea' experience. La Fontelina requires a 2025–2026 minimum spend of €200 per person (sunbed + lunch + drinks) in high season (29 May–13 September), per their own website. Da Luigi ai Faraglioni lists €115 per person (sunbed + restaurant credit) and adds a €10-per-person tender fee each way if you arrive from Marina Piccola by boat. Lido del Faro posts €100 per person. An Instagram summary widely shared on Facebook lists La Fontelina at €190 minimum spend in 2025. TripAdvisor review titled 'Capri scam - Restaurant La Fontelina' documents first-hand sticker shock. Travelers frequently ask in traveler reports for 'a cheaper beach club within walking distance of Capri shops' and locals reply that one does not exist. How to avoid: Confirm the exact per-person minimum spend in writing (email or WhatsApp from the club) before you commit to the boat ride. For La Fontelina, expect €200/person minimum in peak season; for Da Luigi, expect €115/person plus €20 round-trip tender. Free alternatives: Bagni di Tiberio (small fee only, no minimum), Marina Piccola's free pebble beach strip between the two paid lidos, and the Faro lighthouse rocks. Ask whether sunbed rental counts toward the minimum or is added on top — policies vary by club and by season. Book online in advance for Luigi ai Faraglioni through the official site; walk-ins are often refused in July–August.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — The Anacapri Open-Top Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Capri's signature open-top convertible 'Co.Ta.Ca' taxis (Cooperativa Tassisti Capresi) have fixed rates posted on the company's website: Marina Grande → Capri Town €17 (1–4 pax + 1 bag) or €22 (5–6 pax + 2 bags); Marina Grande → Anacapri €23 (1–4 pax). A TripAdvisor Capri Forum thread reports visitors routinely quoted €25–€35 for the same Marina Grande → Anacapri ride, with one Facebook group response recommending '€35, worth splitting with another couple' — roughly 50% above the posted Co.Ta.Ca. rate. Unlicensed or extra-passenger surcharges are a common variant; private 'tour' packages quoting €100–€150 for a 90-minute island loop are technically tours, not taxi fares, and fall outside the posted fixed-rate table. How to avoid: Use the Co.Ta.Ca. posted fixed rates: Marina Grande → Capri Town €17/€22, Marina Grande → Anacapri €23, Capri Town → Anacapri around €20. Ask the driver to confirm the fixed fare before the car moves and point to the Co.Ta.Ca. sticker / rate card. The funicolare from Marina Grande to Capri Town is €2.20 and runs every 15 minutes — use it unless you have heavy luggage. ATC bus 'Marina Grande → Anacapri' costs €2.20 and runs every 15–30 minutes. Keep the receipt; file complaints with the Comune di Capri or Co.Ta.Ca. at capritaxi.it for any driver who refuses the fixed fare. For group tours, book directly with Co.Ta.Ca. online for their official tour rates rather than negotiating street-side.

Scam alert in Capri, Italy — Aggressive Touting & 'Accerchiamento' of Tourists (scam_approach, severity: high). A Repubblica Napoli story dated April 7, 2026 — 'Capri, multe fino a 500 euro per barcaioli e ristoratori che accerchiano i turisti' — reports that the Comune di Capri introduced a new ordinance imposing fines up to €500 on boat operators and restaurant touts who surround, follow, or aggressively solicit tourists stepping off the Marina Grande hydrofoil. A parallel Metropolis story (April 7, 2026) covers the 'turismo molesto' fines. A March 13, 2026 Metropolis investigation documents a 28-year-old tour guide from Castellammare being physically beaten in the Piazzetta by a local shopkeeper angered at competing commerce — evidence that aggressive commerce on Capri has tipped into violence. Touts at Marina Grande funnel confused arrivals into overpriced Blue Grotto tours, inflated taxi rides, and restaurants that pay commissions — the touts themselves are now illegal, and the new €500 fine regime is the tell. How to avoid: Walk directly from the hydrofoil past all touts at Marina Grande with your itinerary already set. The funicolare entrance is 80 meters from the pier — head for it. If a tout follows you after you say 'no grazie,' note their face and report to Polizia Locale at +39 081-837-1011 — the April 2026 ordinance makes their approach a €500 fine. Never accept 'come with me, special price' offers for boats or restaurants from anyone not stationed at a signed operator counter. Decide your Blue Grotto plan, beach-club booking, and lunch restaurant before you land in Marina Grande — touts exploit hesitation. If a shopkeeper becomes physically threatening, call 112 (Carabinieri) immediately.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Fake Cinque Terre Card Seller (money, severity: high). Informal sellers in vests at Riomaggiore and Monterosso trail entrances and La Spezia Centrale station insist tourists need a €35–€50 'Trekking Plus' pass when the official Cinque Terre Treno MS Card on the Parco Nazionale's 2026 price list runs €17.30 (low-attendance band) to €32.50 (high-season Band C). The real card already covers both unlimited regional trains Levanto–La Spezia and the Sentiero Azzurro. A Rick Steves forum thread ('Tourists charged €15 for Cinque Terre: where do you pay?') documents the confusion scammers exploit; scammers also invent 'emergency trekking passes' when trails like the Manarola–Corniglia lungomare close for landslides. How to avoid: Buy the card at card.parconazionale5terre.it online, at Trenitalia machines inside La Spezia Centrale, Levanto, or any of the five village stations, or at staffed Parco Nazionale Welcome Centers — never from sidewalk sellers. Cross-check today's price against the park's fare sheet (€17.30–€32.50 for a 2026 adult 1-day). If a trail section is closed, take a €3 regional train to bypass it instead of buying an 'emergency pass'. Save a phone screenshot of your purchased card and 2026 price band.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Trenitalia Digital-Ticket Check-In Fine (transport, severity: high). Trenitalia regional digital tickets require an in-app 'check-in' press on travel day before the conductor's scan will validate — traveler reports document a €60 fine issued to a family who showed their email QR without checking in, and follow-up reports repeat the complaint. The Cinque Terre Express runs every 20 minutes 14 March to 1 November 2026, each leg is roughly €3, and static email PDFs or Google Wallet passes are consistently fined on board. Italo and high-speed Frecciarossa tickets do not require the same check-in. How to avoid: Install the Trenitalia app, open it on travel day, and tap 'Check-in' on each regional ticket before boarding — show the dynamic (animated) QR, not a static screenshot. If you prefer paper, validate printed tickets in the green platform machines before boarding. The physical Cinque Terre Treno MS Card sidesteps this entirely. If fined, pay on the train for a 50% reduction.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Ferry Ticket Confusion at Monterosso & Riomaggiore (transport, severity: high). Navigazione Golfo dei Poeti publishes a €30 one-way single Monterosso–Riomaggiore, a €28 afternoon-only round-trip (valid from 2pm), and a more expensive multi-stop day pass — confusion between them is documented on Rick Steves Travel Forum and Cinque Terre Facebook traveler threads. Corniglia has no ferry dock (cliff geography), so passes pitched as 'all five villages' exclude it silently. Street sellers hawk non-official tickets on the promenades; rough-sea suspensions get swapped for non-refundable dated tickets. How to avoid: Buy only at Navigazione Golfo dei Poeti kiosks at each village harbour or online at navigazionegolfodeipoeti.it. Confirm before paying whether the ticket is a one-way single, an afternoon round-trip, or a multi-stop day pass. Plan a train leg for Corniglia since no ferry stops there. For multi-village hopping, the €17.30–€32.50 Cinque Terre Treno MS Card is far cheaper than any ferry pass.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Manarola & Vernazza Parking Extortion (transport, severity: high). All five Cinque Terre villages are ZTL-restricted to residents — traveler reports state bluntly 'Vernazza, and all of Cinque Terre, has restricted parking and driving for residents only.' Men in reflective vests flag approaching cars into informal lots on the SP370 above Manarola and Vernazza, collecting €30–€40 cash without authority. Legitimate comune lots sit outside the ZTL at €3–€4/hour. Il Secolo XIX's April 2026 Pasqua reportage documents 85%+ occupancy peaks when informal operators appear. Corriere viaggi's Cinque Terre feature advises 'Alle Cinque Terre si va con il treno … Attenzione alla truffa.' ZTL fines arrive by post weeks later at €80+. How to avoid: Don't drive into Cinque Terre — park at the La Spezia Centrale multi-storey parcheggio or at Levanto and take the €3 regional train. If driving is unavoidable, choose hotels that include guest parking (Levanto, La Spezia) rather than in-village apartments. Use only marked comune lots outside the ZTL with posted hourly rates and ticket machines. Never pay cash to a 'parking attendant' without a printed comune receipt. Watch for ZTL signs (round, red outline) and turn around before entering restricted zones.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Harbourfront "Al Etto" Seafood Trap (overcharging, severity: moderate). Waterfront restaurants in Vernazza harbour, Manarola marina, and Monterosso's Fegina beachfront price fish 'al etto' (per 100g) — at €6–€8 per 100g a 600g branzino runs €36–€48 before a €4–€5 coperto and 15% foreign-card 'servizio' compound the bill. Traveler reports document glossy four-language photo menus with barkers outside, ambiguous per-etto pricing, unrequested pane-acqua-antipasti, and Italian-language Google reviews far below the English ones. Italian law requires menus with prices posted outside — missing menus are a clear tell. Italian-language insider guides (getawayboattour.it) steer diners to inland Manarola spots (Rio Bistrot, Focacceria A Pie De Campu) over harbour-edge venues. How to avoid: Eat one street inland from the harbour — coperto drops from €4–€5 to €2–€2.50 within a minute's walk uphill. Photograph the outside menu and ask 'il pesce, quanto costa intero?' (whole-fish price) before ordering al etto. Confirm 'mi conferma il coperto e se c'è servizio?' at seating. Sort Google Maps reviews by 'Most Recent' in Italian — a 4.5-Italian / 3.8-English split signals the reverse of a tourist trap. Favour trattorie and osterie with handwritten daily menus over 80-item photo menus.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Focaccia-by-Weight Overcut (overcharging, severity: moderate). Ligurian focaccia is legitimately sold 'al peso' (by weight), but tourist-focused focaccerie in Monterosso, Riomaggiore, and Manarola routinely cut slices 2–3x larger than what a customer gestured at, weigh on scales angled away from view, and announce the total only after wrapping — traveler reports document Monterosso's focaccia reputation and the weight-cut mechanic across Italy. Focaccia averages €12–€18/kg at a legitimate shop; a €9 slice is typically 550–700g at ~€15/kg — fine if you wanted that much, a trap if you pointed at a 200g piece. The authentic consorzio-protected focaccia belt sits north in Recco and Camogli with posted consortium prices. How to avoid: Say 'solo questo' and point precisely at the exact piece you want before the clerk picks up the knife. Ask 'quanto al chilo?' for the per-kilo price up front. Watch the scale — ask 'mi fa vedere la bilancia, per favore?' if it's angled away. Decline before wrapping: 'è troppo, la metà basta.' For benchmark focaccia, travel north to Recco or Camogli where the col formaggio consorzio posts prices prominently.

Scam alert in Cinque Terre, Italy — The Fake Cinque Terre Apartment Rental (money, severity: moderate). Il Secolo XIX's April 2026 Pasqua reportage documents Cinque Terre hotel occupancy above 85% — exactly the tight-supply, panic-booking window short-term-rental scams exploit. Fake listings on third-party sites, Facebook groups, and direct-email offers request bank wires off-platform and disappear at arrival. TripAdvisor Italy Forum warnings ('SCAM. DO NOT BOOK. Booked it and when I arrived after a long road trip we found the place closed…') repeat across Italy. Two Cinque Terre-specific variants: tiny-village listings (Vernazza ~800 residents, Corniglia ~240) where cross-verification is hard because street-view data is sparse, and Monterosso beachfront listings that appear at Easter and July peaks at half market rate. Italian law requires a CIR/CIN registration code; legitimate listings show it. How to avoid: Book only through Airbnb, Booking.com, or Vrbo with pay-through-platform protection — never wire for a Cinque Terre apartment. Require the host to provide a CIR/CIN code before paying; check it on the Liguria regional registry. Use Google Street View to verify the building entry (villages are small enough to locate). Ask for an in-platform photo of the entrance, intercom label, and keybox — scammers refuse. Refuse any cash-only 'city fee' surprise on arrival above the posted local tourism-tax rate.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The San Lorenzo Fake-Leather Market (counterfeit, severity: high). San Lorenzo market stalls and surrounding leather shops sell imported Made-in-China PU/faux-leather goods and counterfeit Gucci/Prada/Balenciaga/LV/Fendi bags as 'genuine Italian leather.' Local residents warn 'every item you see outside the central market and center roads is cheap fake stuff created to scam tourists.' Guardia di Finanza cases: a San Lorenzo stall arrest (3 Italians arrested, 1 Chinese denounced); a €100,000 counterfeit-bag seizure in the historic center (4 Chinese denounced); a 49-person 'filiera del falso' investigation copying Armani/Balenciaga/Celine/Fendi/Givenchy/Gucci/LV/Prada; plus Campi Bisenzio and Osmannoro pelletteria raids grossing up to ~€1 million. Traveler reports document a 'pay-but-never-shipped' variant at a Florence leather store. How to avoid: Buy only from established Florentine workshops: Scuola del Cuoio (Santa Croce monastery), Peruzzi, Madova, Bojola, or Il Bisonte. Ignore San Lorenzo stalls unless you want a cheap souvenir; lowball aggressively. Never buy 'designer' brands from Florence stalls — all are counterfeit and Guardia di Finanza seizes them routinely. Carry purchases out in person; refuse any 'we'll ship it home' offer. Price-check against Scuola del Cuoio's online catalogue before paying over €150.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — Duomo & Battistero Pickpocket Duos (pickpocket, severity: high). Two-person pickpocket teams target tourists' backpacks and bags in Piazza del Duomo, Piazza San Giovanni and the Via Calzaiuoli/Via de' Pecori/Via dei Vecchietti/Via de' Tornabuoni corridor. Arrest record: March 16, 2026 La Nazione (2 Bulgarian women, 23, Via dei Vecchietti); March 2025 La Nazione (3 offenders aged 71/55/31, Italian/Hungarian/Romanian, Via Calzaiuoli); August 28, 2024 La Nazione (2 Bulgarian women 28 and 36, Via de' Pecori, €730 recovered); June 5, 2023 La Nazione (Romanian couple 47 and 49, Via de' Tornabuoni, €900 stolen). Tour guide Marco Verzi (Federagit Confesercenti Firenze) reported a pickpocket's threat: 'Se mi rovini il lavoro ti taglio la gola.' How to avoid: Wear your backpack on your chest in Piazza del Duomo and Via Calzaiuoli — zippers toward your sternum. Never carry wallet/phone/passport in outer pockets; use inside zip pockets, a money belt, or a body pouch. Compose Duomo photos before stopping — take the photo, pocket the phone, then look up. If anyone enters your body space, step back one pace and put a hand on your bag. Shout 'ladri!' the instant you feel a brush — Florence Carabinieri on patrol make fast arrests.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The Santa Maria Novella Station Pickpocket Ring (pickpocket, severity: high). Coordinated pickpocket teams and hustlers work Santa Maria Novella (SMN) platforms, underground passages, ticket-machine hall, taxi queue and immediate piazzas. A late-2025 local PSA describes nightly robberies 'for the last three nights in a row… someone screaming, crying, realizing they've just been robbed.' A February 12, 2026 ANSA report documents a 19-year-old arrested at SMN with an elderly Florentine's silverware, €250 cash, antique coins and two Beretta pistols stolen via a 'finto poliziotto' scam. Taxi queue issue: April 2025 traveler reports flag an 'undeclared strike' where drivers refuse short fares from the rank. How to avoid: Exit via the main Piazza della Stazione side, not the rear. Use only the signed official taxi rank or walk 120m to the Alamanni tram stop (T1/T2, €1.70). Use only Trenitalia or Italo apps or operator-branded ticket machines — never let a 'helper' touch your card. Keep luggage on the facing end-of-carriage rack on Frecciarossa/Italo. Walk directly from platform to street; consult your phone outside the station with your back to a pillar.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The "Tre Campanelle" Shell Game at Ponte Vecchio (distraction, severity: high). Three-shell/three-card street gambling scam with accomplice 'winners' in the crowd. Operators work in teams of 6–7 (one mazziere plus compari). January 12, 2026 Repubblica Firenze: Baschi Verdi denouncements at Via de' Cerretani/Via dei Rondinello. November 17, 2025 Corriere Fiorentino: undercover Finanza agents in Piazza del Duomo fined a Romanian operator €400. Firenze Today documents Ponte Vecchio and Piazzale Michelangelo operations. San Lorenzo shopkeepers funded 50+ bilingual 'Il gioco è una truffa!!!' placards. A Corriere Fiorentino first-person piece documents the truffatori physically shoving a witness who warned an Asian tourist. How to avoid: Do not stop to watch, bet, or stand within three meters of any shell-game mat at Ponte Vecchio, Piazza del Duomo, Borgo San Lorenzo or Piazzale Michelangelo. Report live mats to Guardia di Finanza (117). Ignore friendly 'tourists' who claim to know the trick — they are compari. Warn other tourists verbally but do not physically engage operators. Trust San Lorenzo's bilingual warning placards.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The Outdoor Restaurant & Mercato Centrale Bag-Snatch (theft, severity: high). Bags hung on chair backs at outdoor tables and left on Mercato Centrale communal benches are snatched by passing pedestrians or distraction-team accomplices. La Nazione (September 20, 2024): tourist pickpocketed during lunch at a Florence pizzeria. La Nazione's shopkeeper round-up flags Osteria dei Buongustai (Via de' Cerchi) where Japanese diners' bag was taken during peak lunch, Fioreria Signoria ('È un continuo borseggiare turisti'), Eugenio Calzature (Via del Proconsolo, €300 taken from the register), and Le Vanità perfumery ('Quasi tutti i giorni ho ladri in negozi'). Mercato Centrale snatches occur even in non-crowded moments. How to avoid: Always place your bag on the floor with one strap looped around your chair leg or ankle — never on the chair back or an empty seat. Inside Mercato Centrale, keep your bag on your lap or in a chest-worn daypack. Sit with your back to a wall, facing foot traffic. Leave your passport in the hotel safe. Freeze cards in-app immediately if a bag disappears — the cash-out window is 3–10 minutes.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The Piazza della Signoria Coperto & Tourist-Menu Trap (overcharging, severity: moderate). Restaurants facing the major piazze add unmarked per-person coperto (often above €3), a 12–15% automatic 'servizio' on foreign cards, unrequested pane/acqua/olive/antipasti, and fish or steak priced 'al etto' (per 100g) that arrives as 400–700g portions. A variant splits the bill into part-cash/part-card to dodge VAT on the cash portion. Traveler reports distinguish two severities: a 'few restaurants where you will leave feeling as if you've been scammed — deceptive prices, aggressive waiters' versus a broader ring that is 'modestly overpriced.' Italian law requires every restaurant to post a full menu with prices outside — a missing menu is legally non-compliant. How to avoid: Walk 5 minutes off the Signoria/Duomo axis — Oltrarno (Piazza Santo Spirito, San Frediano), Sant'Ambrogio, or streets north of Sant'Ambrogio market are locally recommended. Photograph the outside-posted menu before sitting; if fish/steak are 'al etto' only, ask for per-gram confirmation in writing. Ask the waiter to confirm coperto and servizio at seating. Refuse unsolicited bread/water/antipasti with 'niente grazie.' Trust Italian-language Most-Recent Google reviews over English reviews.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The SMN Taxi "Strike" & Airport Flat-Rate Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Florence airport (FLR/Peretola) drivers quote 'flat fares' above the official €22 daytime or €25.30 night/holiday fixed rate; SMN rank drivers refuse short fares during an 'undeclared strike' (April 2025 community PSA: '30 minutes' wait, one traveler had to have a hotel call). 'Card reader is broken' scam forces ATM detours with driver watching the PIN. Short-change tricks (a handed €50 substituted for a €10 via sleight of hand, per traveler reports). Unlicensed NCCs approaching at SMN and FLR offering 'fisso' rides are another layer. How to avoid: From FLR Peretola take the Tramvia T2 to SMN Alamanni stop — €1.70, ~22 minutes, nothing to negotiate. For taxis, use only official white vehicles at the signed rank and confirm €22 daytime / €25.30 night/Sunday airport fixed fare before closing the door. Call 055-4242 or 055-4390 for radio taxis or use itTaxi/FreeNow apps. Always demand a ricevuta. Refuse any ATM detour — pay the posted fare in cash, photograph the taxi number, and report to 055-055.

Scam alert in Florence, Italy — The Uffizi "Free" Bracelet, Rose & Painting Ambush (distraction, severity: low). 'Free' bracelets tied on tourists' wrists then cashed for €10–€20; roses pressed into partners' hands with a follow-up €15 demand; cheap prints laid on the pavement in tourist walking paths with a scream for €50 'damages' if you step on one. One traveler wrote of the prints version: 'They plop these big mats on the ground right in the path and if you step on one they try and get you to pay for it… mostly saw men doing this in front of the museum where David was kept.' Firenze Today documents a YouTuber physically assaulted after denouncing the prints scam in the historic center — refusing is fine, engaging or filming can turn into confrontation. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets in Piazza del Duomo and Piazzale degli Uffizi — no outstretched palm, no wrist to tie a bracelet on. Say 'no grazie' firmly, do not make eye contact after, and keep walking. If a bracelet gets on, pull it off and drop it — they rarely chase. Hand back a rose within the first second or leave it on the table with 'non lo voglio.' Do not engage or film the 'painting' operators — just step around the prints.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Bellagio/Varenna "Taxi Abusivo" Malpensa Flat-Rate (transport, severity: high). Unlicensed drivers (tassisti abusivi) meet flights at Malpensa and Bergamo and quote flat €150–€250 fares to Bellagio or Varenna, bypassing licensed NCC/taxi rules. La Provincia di Como's July 26, 2024 'Bellagio, lotta ai taxi abusivi' report documents four abusivi stopped in a single week charging '150 euro da Malpensa' without safety or professional credentials — fines are €173 each and the vehicle is seized. A June 29, 2025 La Provincia Unica TV story documents the same pattern in Varenna, where polizia locale caught abusivi in flagrante, seizing cars on the spot. A June 5, 2024 La Provincia follow-up details three more Bellagio busts in a week. Drivers often text-message via WhatsApp and meet tourists off-airport. How to avoid: Book a licensed NCC in writing with a VAT number before you fly — Malpensa-to-Bellagio is 95km/~1h45 and legitimate fares run €160–€220 with a receipt and company logo on the car. From Malpensa, the cheapest legit path is Malpensa Express to Milano Centrale (€13) then Trenord to Varenna-Esino (€6.70) plus NLC ferry to Bellagio (€5.50) — about 2h15 total. Never accept a WhatsApp-arranged 'taxi' whose driver has no posted license. Refuse any car without a company name on the door or a visible NCC/taxi license card on the dashboard. Demand a ricevuta fiscale at drop-off; abusivi can't issue one.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Varenna–Bellagio Water-Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Private water-taxi operators quote €200–€350 for a 15-minute Varenna-Bellagio crossing that costs €5.50 on the public NLC ferry. A Visit Lake Como Facebook thread documents '€250 for one way Varenna to Bellagio, and if you miss the allocated time, no refunds.' A TripAdvisor review of Comolakeboats (Domaso) titled 'Tourist scam and rip off' describes the customer losing €380 after the operator refused to deliver the booked service. Barindelli Taxi Boat publicly lists 1-hour Bellagio villa cruises at €350 and 1.5h tours at higher rates — legal, but routinely mistaken for 'taxi' pricing by tourists expecting a transfer. An Espansione TV / Como enforcement operation documented five taxi-boat operators with irregularities on Lake Como, with fines up to €1,200. How to avoid: Use the public Navigazione Lago di Como (NLC) ferry — Bellagio–Varenna–Menaggio is a €5.50 single for passengers, with a hydrofoil option for about €11. Check official timetables at navigazionelaghi.it. Never accept a 'water taxi' quote at the pier without it posted on a price board in euro with VAT — legitimate operators like Taxi Boat Varenna publish rate cards. Ignore drivers who approach you with 'we can take you now, ferry is full' pitches, especially in peak-season evenings after the ferry stops running at 7pm. Pay only after you see a receipt with the company's P.IVA, and never wire a deposit in advance for a 'reserved taxi boat.'

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Bellagio ZTL & Parking Ambush (overcharging, severity: high). Bellagio's ZTL (limited-traffic zone) and Faggeto Lario's unofficial lots generate a high-volume fine stream and private-lot disputes that tourists don't learn about until months after returning home. QuiComo's April 13, 2025 'Bellagio record multe ZTL 2024' and the April 2025 Mediaset/Tgcom24 feature report near-record ZTL fine income for 2024. An April 2026 QuiComo report on province-wide fines documents €5.5M in total traffic sanctions in 2025 across the Como area, with Bellagio called out as the 'caso clamoroso.' A separate April 5, 2026 QuiComo story, 'Lago di Como, il paradosso dei parcheggi privati,' documents tourists parking in Faggeto Lario private property, cutting chains, and ignoring signs — and private lot owners charging €10–€20/hour 'tariffs' with no receipt. A ComoZero report details tour buses being fined on the SS Regina coast road for illegal stops. How to avoid: Do not drive into Bellagio's historic center — the ZTL is camera-monitored and the fine is issued by post up to a year later, typically €95–€130 plus charges. Park at the Lido di Bellagio lot (signposted on the approach) or leave the car in Varenna and take the NLC ferry. If you must use a private lot, photograph the price signage and get a timestamped printed receipt — refuse any 'cash only, no ricevuta' attendant. Never cut a private-property chain or move a 'proprietà privata' sign; fines and trespass charges apply. On the SS Regina coast road, park only in blue-lined municipal bays and check the parcometro app.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Bellagio "Petition Against Drugs" Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). Young men approach tourists on Bellagio's waterfront and Salita Serbelloni asking them to sign a clipboard 'petition against drugs' or a deaf-community donation sheet — both scripts are documented cover for pocket- and bag-pickpocketing. TripAdvisor's Bellagio Forum thread 'Beware — Petition against drugs scam spreads to Bellagio' (June 2014) describes a traveler approached twice in one afternoon by young males with the same script. Traveler reports confirm the same routine: 'the sign here against drugs scam is alive and well in Lake Como.' The script mirrors the scam that police in Milan and Venice have prosecuted for years: the clipboard and chatter occupy your eyeline while a second hand or accomplice pulls a wallet or phone from the pocket or bag. How to avoid: Never stop to sign anything a stranger hands you on a Lake Como waterfront or on Salita Serbelloni — the script is almost always cover for theft or an aggressive cash 'donation' demand. Reply 'no grazie' without breaking stride and keep your hand on your bag. Carry phones in zipped interior pockets, not back pockets, when walking Bellagio's main drag between Piazza Mazzini and the Grand Hotel Villa Serbelloni. Use a crossbody bag worn on the lake-wall side so pickpockets have no approach angle. If you feel someone pushing a clipboard into your chest, step back one full pace — that is the physical cue for the second-hand grab.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Lungo-Lario "Menu with Lake View" Surcharge (overcharging, severity: moderate). Lakefront restaurants in Bellagio, Varenna, and Como hit foreign diners with unmarked per-person coperto, auto-applied 10–15% servizio, and fish priced 'al etto' that arrives as a 400–600g portion billed at four to five times the menu figure. A 2024 community 'Lake Como FAQs — A Local's Guide' warns that 'most lakeside places with signs in English (and sometimes pictures of the dishes) are touristy spots.' Explorecomolake.com's 'Come evitare le trappole per turisti sul Lago di Como' lists tourist menus and questionable service charges as the top tourist trap. Traveler threads 'Bellagio is over-rated' and 'Best food in Bellagio' name lake-front restaurants as 'terrible tourist traps' with poor food quality. Travelers also document Amalfi-coast-style price gouging with comparable '€18 glass of wine' incidents around Lake Como. How to avoid: Walk five minutes uphill from any Lake Como waterfront — in Bellagio, streets like Salita Serbelloni and Via Garibaldi have honest trattorias; in Varenna, head uphill from Piazza San Giorgio toward Vezio; in Como, leave Piazza Cavour for Via Carloni (a community Cardamomo pizza recommendation). Photograph the posted menu outside before you sit — Italian law requires it. Ask 'quanto costa al etto?' before ordering fish, and request a ballpark weight. Refuse any 'pane, acqua, antipasto' you didn't order — Italian law lets you decline. Sort Google reviews by Italian and Most Recent; a venue rated 4.5+ by Italian reviewers is rarely a trap.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Navigazione Laghi "Wrong Ticket" Trap (transport, severity: moderate). The public Navigazione Lago di Como (NLC) system sells four fare classes — battello (slow, ~€11 Como–Bellagio), aliscafo/freccia (fast hydrofoil, ~€16), ferry (car ferry, passengers only €5.50 Bellagio–Varenna), and a daily 'giornaliero' pass — and tourists routinely buy the wrong one, arriving at a pier for a boat that doesn't stop there or validating a ticket that's already expired. Multiple TripAdvisor reviews ('Misleading ferry tickets,' August 2023; 'Avoid this operator,' August 2022) document overcrowded ferries, confusing website, and rude service. One 2025 traveler wrote of the system: 'a disaster, a mess with tickets, always horrible queues.' La Provincia di Como's May 31, 2023 'Turismo a Como? Battelli pieni, non si può salire' report confirms that peak-summer boats hit capacity and tourists with valid tickets are turned away. How to avoid: Buy tickets only at the official NLC biglietteria (ticket office) at each pier or through the new NaviTAP contactless tap-at-the-turnstile system — never from a tout at the pier. Check navigazionelaghi.it for live timetables and line letters; Bellagio–Varenna–Menaggio is line C1 (car ferry, passenger €5.50), Como–Colico is the main northbound line with slow and fast services. Validate battello/aliscafo tickets at the yellow machine before boarding — unvalidated tickets void the fare. In July–August, arrive 30 minutes before the scheduled departure; peak boats fill and late passengers are left at the dock. Never buy a 'hop-on hop-off lake pass' from a third-party kiosk; NLC's own giornaliero is the only official day pass.

Scam alert in Lake Como, Italy — The Fake Clooney-Villa Rental & Airbnb Redirect (money, severity: high). Lake Como attracts two flavors of rental fraud: the classic fake-Airbnb redirect that moves payment off-platform to a bank wire, and the higher-end 'celebrity villa' scam that sells imaginary stays at or near George Clooney's Villa Oleandra in Laglio. The 2010 Milan court case against Vincenzo Cannalire, Francesco Galdelli and Vanja Goggi — who impersonated Clooney, used forged Versace and Armani paperwork, and sold fake access to his lifestyle — established that Clooney-themed fraud has a documented prosecution history on Lake Como. A 2022 Metro UK report details Adam Bailey losing £3,000 on a fake 'Italian villa' Airbnb listing for a family holiday. TripAdvisor Lake Como Forum's 'Accommodation scam; private owners' thread documents an off-platform redirect from Homeaway/Vrbo that moved a booking to direct payment and left the tourist with no listing at arrival. Local scam-alert Facebook groups document fake-Airbnb lookalike sites asking for bank transfer. How to avoid: Book only via Airbnb, Booking.com, or Vrbo's in-app chat and payment — never by email redirect, WhatsApp, or bank transfer. If a host claims Airbnb 'is down' or sends you a link that looks like Airbnb but has a different domain, it is a phishing site; close it and re-contact through the verified app. Reverse-image-search every property photo; stock/reused photos are an instant red flag. No legitimate Lake Como rental offers 'tours' or 'stays' at George Clooney's Villa Oleandra — he does not rent it, and any such offer is fraud. For villa rentals above €200/night, call the property's listed landline (not a WhatsApp number) and confirm the reservation in Italian before paying. Budget for Lake Como's tourist tax (€1–€5/night depending on comune and hotel class) — a host who adds it as a surprise cash 'city fee' on arrival is often pocketing it.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Sirmione Tourist-Trap Markup (€75 Lunch, €8 Gelato) (overcharging, severity: high). Lake-facing restaurants and gelaterias on the Sirmione peninsula price at extreme tourist markups. A June 3, 2025 Corriere Brescia cronaca piece 'Una giornata a Sirmione tra code, bellezza e... salassi' documents €75 for a single lunch and €8 for one gelato scoop. A viral 2025 Instagram reel shows a visitor quoted '3.50 per scoop' with escalating upcharges. A May 2025 traveler-forum 'Ultra-overtourism — Extreme Edition' thread describes ~14 million annual visitors funneled through a narrow peninsula as 'a congested trap' with spintoni and code interminabili, and Il Giorno's 'Sirmione invasa dai turisti' confirms the pattern. How to avoid: Walk at least 300 meters inland from the castle or back toward the drawbridge before eating — Corriere frames peninsula-center prices as salassi (bloodlettings), not normal Italian prices. Confirm single-scoop and double-scoop gelato prices at the counter before ordering. Photograph the posted menu outside (required by Italian law) before sitting; ask the server to weigh fish before cooking. Prefer Desenzano, Peschiera, or Lazise. Always demand a ricevuta fiscale.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Fake "Private Boat Tour" Facebook Deposit Scam (money, severity: high). 'Local captain' scammers pitch private Lake Garda boat tours via Facebook Lake Garda groups, Instagram DMs, and direct waterfront approaches, then collect an off-platform deposit (bank wire, PayPal friends-and-family, Revolut) and vanish. The Lake Garda Italy Facebook group has published repeated near-identical fraud alerts since 2023 — one 2023 alert posted across multiple groups naming 'Private boat tour scam in Lake Garda' as a running thread. Navigazione Laghi (NLG) at navigazionelaghi.it is the only official state-sanctioned public-line ferry operator; legitimate private charters all publish a P.IVA. How to avoid: Use only platforms with refund guarantees — GetYourGuide, Viator, Airbnb Experiences — or book direct through Navigazione Laghi for public ferries. For private charters, verify the captain's P.IVA on verifica-partita-iva.it before paying any deposit. Refuse any 'pay off-platform to avoid fees' request — that exact phrasing is the clearest scam tell. Cross-check against the Lake Garda Italy Facebook group running list of flagged pages. Pay by credit card through the platform only.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Bardolino/Garda Fake Deaf-Mute Petition Pickpocket (pickpocket, severity: high). Organized crews on the Veronese lungolago approach tourists with clipboards and 'I am deaf-mute' petitions for 'children with disabilities,' guiding victims' hands to sign while an accomplice pickpockets. L'Arena documents Polizia locale di Bardolino intercepting three of four falsi sordomuti during a coordinated sweep (with one officer injured); a separate L'Arena Garda-Baldo piece — 'Nicotra, un giorno da sceriffo' — documents the sindaco personally stopping two fake deaf-mutes. Gardapost reports Carabinieri di Lazise charging two travelling arrotini with truffa and danneggiamento in a related scam. How to avoid: Do not sign any clipboard petition on a Lake Garda lungolago — refuse with 'no, grazie' and keep walking. Keep phone and wallet out of back pockets and outer bag pouches on the Bardolino or Garda lungolago. If seated at a café and approached, keep one hand on your bag and step back from physical contact. If robbed, call 112 and report to Polizia locale di Bardolino, Garda, or Carabinieri di Lazise. Daily-use wallet €40–€60 only; flat pouch under your shirt for cards and passport.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Grotte di Catullo "Combo Tour" Ticket Markup (overcharging, severity: moderate). Touts at the Sirmione drawbridge and castle arch sell 'skip-the-line combo tours' bundling the Grotte di Catullo with the Scaligero castle, a peninsula train, and/or an NLG ferry at €20–€45 per person. The real on-site adult Grotte ticket is €6 intero / €3 ridotto (TripAdvisor 2024–2025 reviews and beniculturali.it confirm), bought at Piazzale Orti Manara 4, 25019 Sirmione (BS), +39 030 916157. A January 2025 Gardapost piece documents free guided tour days included with the €6 ticket — meaning there is never a real 'skip-the-line' value to sell. How to avoid: Buy Grotte di Catullo tickets only at the on-site box office (Piazzale Orti Manara 4) or via the official beniculturali.it booking portal — never from a tout. Walk from the Sirmione drawbridge to the Grotte in 20–25 minutes along the signed peninsula path. For guided tours, book a licensed Regione Lombardia guide (tessera di guida turistica). Most of the peninsula is free to walk without any ticket; Spiaggia Giamaica and the external ruins view cost zero.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Malcesine Funivia Queue-Jump & Repeat-Ticket Hustle (ticket_scam, severity: moderate). Unofficial resellers on Via Navene Vecchia and the Malcesine lungolago sell 'skip-the-line' Funivia Malcesine Monte Baldo cable car tickets at €35–€40 (above the Funivie del Baldo lower-station rate) that turn out to be ordinary or invalidated tickets, plus 'guided Monte Baldo hike' bundles that mark up the signposted free Monte Altissimo trail by €50–€80. TripAdvisor's 'Warning Mount Baldo Wait Times!' Lake Garda Forum thread documents legitimate mid-season mid-morning waits of 3+ hours with no time-warnings posted at queue entry — enabling the hustle. How to avoid: Buy cable car tickets only at the Funivia Malcesine lower-station office or online at funiviedelbaldo.it. Arrive at 08:00 opening to avoid the 3-hour mid-morning waits TripAdvisor users document. Check the timetables and fares page before travelling (30-minute cadence is conditional). Do not pay for a 'guided Monte Baldo hike' — the Monte Altissimo trail is signposted and free. In peak summer, buy a dated time-slot ticket online in advance so resellers have nothing to sell you.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Lake Garda Holiday Rental Deposit Scam (money, severity: high). Peak-summer 'villa with lake view' listings on Facebook Marketplace, Instagram, and off-platform Airbnb/Booking messages demand wire-transfer deposits, then disappear. A 2023 Lake Garda Italy Facebook group post documents a family's full deposit lost after 'booking directly with accommodation provider.' A 2025 traveler-forum Sirmione overtourism thread identifies short-term rentals as 'the cancer of Lake Garda,' confirming the listings ecosystem has grown to a scale where fake listings hide among real ones. The Airbnb Community 'Long term rental safety concern' thread documents the off-platform wire variant. How to avoid: Book only through Airbnb, Booking.com, Hotels.com, or Vrbo — all have pay-through-platform guarantees. Refuse any off-platform payment request, full stop — even from a 5-star host. Verify the property on Google Street View, Instagram geo-tags, and TripAdvisor photos before paying. Pay by credit card (not debit). Budget for Lombardia/Veneto tourism tax (€1–€4 per person per night); demand a ricevuta fiscale for any cash city-fee or pay by card only.

Scam alert in Lake Garda, Italy — The Verona Airport → Garda Unlicensed NCC Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Unlicensed NCC drivers approach arrivals at Verona Villafranca 'Valerio Catullo' airport (VRN) with 'taxi?' offers, quoting flat rates of €90–€120 for rides that metered official Radio Taxi Verona (white-painted, 045.532.222) deliver at roughly €50–€60 to Bardolino, Lazise, or Peschiera. Variants include 'broken credit-card reader' ATM scams and 'deviazione' fake detours. A BresciaToday piece — 'Vestone: attenti alla truffa dei finti turisti rimasti senza benzina' — documents a Lake Garda variant where foreigners ran a fake stranded-tourist pitch. How to avoid: Use only white-painted Radio Taxi Verona (045.532.222) vehicles at the signed rank outside the terminal — confirm the metered ride before closing the door. Cheaper alternative: ATV Aerobus service 199 to Verona Porta Nuova (€6), then regional train to Peschiera/Desenzano/Lazise (€3–€5). Pre-book through GetYourGuide, Welcome Pickups, or a hotel shuttle with posted rate. Demand a ricevuta fiscale. Refuse any ATM detour; complain to the Polizia di Stato VRN airport office.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Duomo Bracelet & "3-Euro Selfie" Trap (street_scam, severity: high). Men in Piazza del Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II flick friendship bracelets onto tourists' wrists or offer to take their photo 'only 3 euros,' then demand €20+ or pass the phone to an accomplice. Milano Today's viral 'truffa dei selfie' video documents the €3 selfie pitch; Corriere della Sera published a British tourist's TikTok warning recounting the same pitch at Castello Sforzesco and the Duomo. Il Giorno documents 100 Antiborseggio arrests in 100 days in 2025 working this exact 200-meter radius. How to avoid: Treat bracelet and selfie men as invisible — do not stop, do not make eye contact, do not reply. Keep arms close to your torso crossing Piazza Duomo (bracelet only works if you reflexively catch). Never hand your phone to a stranger. If a bracelet is tied on, walk away with it on your wrist — do not pay. Shout 'polizia!' if someone refuses to release your arm; plainclothes Antiborseggio patrol the Duomo.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The M1 / M3 Metro Pickpocket Ring at Duomo (pickpocket, severity: high). Three-to-five-person teams swarm passengers on the M1 red and M3 yellow lines — especially Cairoli–Duomo and the Duomo mezzanine — using a 'fall and help' distraction while accomplices unzip bags. A firsthand traveler-forum victim post titled 'I was pickpocketed on the train from Cairoli to Duomo' documents the domino-push MO. Corriere Milano published a September 2024 first-person account. Repubblica April 2023 records a 34-year-old punched in the eye at the Duomo mezzanine for warning passengers. Milan's own metro PA now warns 'attenzione, pickpocket!' How to avoid: Wear backpacks on your chest, not your back, on M1 and M3. Keep phone/wallet in inside jacket or front trouser pockets. Buy tickets only from ATM Milano machines, newsstands, or contactless gates — never from anyone 'selling' tickets near machines. If a group clusters around you as doors close, step off and take the next train. Shout 'polizia!' and press the platform intercom if pickpocketed; Polmetro patrols Duomo in plainclothes.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — Milano Centrale Platform & Luggage-Theft Teams (pickpocket, severity: high). Coordinated teams work Milano Centrale platforms, concourse, and the Galleria delle Carrozze, with fake 'helpers' offering to carry bags or operate ticket machines. A traveler-forum thread titled 'Milano centrale pick pocketing is real' documents a three-person team (two girls + one man) testing a father's backpack zipper within seconds of entering the station. Milano Today documents arrests: three Roma women who pickpocketed Japanese tourists at the Centrale metro; a 22-year-old Moroccan man caught snatching a bag inside the station; a three-year sentence for a July 2016 daylight assault in Via Napo Torriani (near Hotel Berna). How to avoid: Never let anyone touch your luggage inside Milano Centrale — politely refuse all 'help.' On Frecciarossa/Italo, put luggage on the end-of-carriage rack you face rather than overhead. Take only official white Taxi Blu (02.4040) or Autoradio (02.8585) from the signed rank; ignore any 'taxi?' offers inside the hall. Use only operator-logo machines for tickets. Avoid walking Via Napo Torriani alone with luggage in daylight.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Via Dante "Tre Campanelle" Shell Game (scam_game, severity: high). Crews run the 'three bells' shell game and three-card variants on Via Dante, Via Torino, Piazza Cordusio and under the Castello Sforzesco drawbridge, with paid shills as 'winners' luring tourists to bet. A Repubblica Milano April 1, 2026 report documents a tourist losing €500 to the scam on Via Dante; Corriere Milano's September 29, 2025 feature records 125 people denounced by local police in four months between Via Torino and Via Dante, stopped with up to €4,000 in victims' cash. Milano Today documents a Castello Sforzesco three-card variant that ran combined with pickpocketing a US couple — producing five arrests. How to avoid: Recognize the shape on sight — a small crowd around a low table on Via Dante, Via Torino, Cordusio or the Castello approach is almost always tre campanelle. Do not slow down, do not look, do not join. If a stranger steps up beside you and narrates the game, step back two meters — they are there to pickpocket you. Never bet; the operator and the player both commit offenses under Italian law. Report active games to polizia locale at 02.0208. Call 112 immediately if you've lost money — recovery window is minutes.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Malpensa / Linate Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: high). Drivers at Malpensa, Linate and Orio al Serio charge 2–2.5x the posted fixed fare (Malpensa €95, Linate €65 to central Milan in 2025), switch to long-distance tariffs mid-trip, or claim the card reader is 'broken.' A firsthand traveler-forum victim paid €250 from Malpensa (vs €105 then-fixed), with two other Milan-airport victims chiming in below the same comment. Milano Today documents an unlicensed driver without a valid license caught working Malpensa. A 'friendly stranger' variant targets solo travelers inside the MXP arrivals hall. How to avoid: Take the Malpensa Express to Cadorna or Centrale (€13 standard, €20 non-stop; 43–52 min); Linate is €2.20 on M4 metro. For taxis, confirm the posted fixed fare aloud before closing the door ('novantacinque euro, corretto?'). Use only white Taxi Blu or Autoradio at the signed rank. Use FreeNow or itTaxi app for fare-transparent bookings. Refuse ATM detours — Italian law requires card acceptance. If overcharged, pay by card and dispute; Amex chargeback has been documented as working.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Fake Plainclothes-Police ID Check (money, severity: high). Men posing as plainclothes police flash laminated badges, claim to be checking for 'counterfeit notes,' and pocket cash and watches during the 'verification.' Repubblica Milano's January 2017 cronaca documents a Russian tourist couple losing €10,000 in cash and two luxury watches to this MO. Corriere Milano's July 2019 report documents an 11-person crew specializing in Milan fake-police robberies. Milano Today documents a married-couple 'Bonnie e Clyde' crew who ran the scam across Italy with specific Milan incidents. How to avoid: Never hand over wallet, passport, or valuables to anyone not in full uniform inside a police station. Ask to be 'accompanied to the police station' for the check — real officers agree; scammers make excuses. Demand to see the badge at reading distance; compare to Polizia di Stato tessera images on poliziadistato.it. Walk toward a crowded area or a real carabiniere; call 112 while walking. Keep daily wallet separate from passport and main cards.

Scam alert in Milan, Italy — The Navigli Aperitivo Tourist-Trap Bill (overcharging, severity: moderate). Canal-side Navigli aperitivo spots apply unadvertised per-person coperto above €3, auto-applied 10–15% 'servizio' on foreign cards, unrequested pane/acqua/antipasti, and a 'turista menu' at 2–3x local prices. A traveler-forum Navigli recommendations thread contains a flat Milanese warning: 'the Navigli area became a real tourist trap, you still can find quality but they will be priced.' The same Quadrilatero tourist-trap density is documented by Corriere's cronaca archive in the Duomo cluster. Italian law (DL 206/2005) requires publicly displayed price-marked menus; missing fish/steak prices is the clearest tell. How to avoid: Walk one block off the Naviglio Grande towpath — Via Vigevano and Via Savona are locally recommended. Photograph the posted menu outside before sitting.
